text: Κατὰ τὴν θέσει κίνησιν. Sic etiam quæst. 56 ad Thalass. Non satis Picus, in peragendo motu. Reddidi, voluntatis motu, non quod θελήσει velim emendatum, sed quod id, quod sic θέσει, quasi ab extrinseco et factitie est, voluntate est, at in adoptione, qua quis θέσει, non φύσει, in familiam filiumque cooptatur. Sic corpus ad animum efferatur, ejus quasi ratione imbutum, qua voluntate virtutibus excolitur, supra illius, ut corpus est, meritum atque debitum.
anchorLine: τῷ νοῒ τὲ σῶμα κατὰ τὴν θέσει κίνησιν (u)· ἡ δὲ,
en: 'According to positional movement.' So too in question 56 to Thalassius. Picus did not grasp it, [rendering] 'in the moving'. I have rendered it 'by a movement of the will', not because I would emend it to θελήσει ('by will'), but because what is thus θέσει, as if from outside and artificial, is by will, as in adoption, by which someone is taken into a family and made a son by θέσει, not by nature. So the body is carried up to the soul, as if imbued with its reason, by which it is cultivated in will with virtues, above its own deserving and due, as a body.

text: Τῆς ἀληθοῦς θεουργίας. Veram θεουργίαν, seu divinam operationem, videtur hic dicere, quæ sic actione et contemplatione completur, et quasi eminenter utriusque vim habet : sapientiam scilicet, quæ proxima est ad deificationem. Quomodo et in Christo dictam θεουργίαν Dionysio, quin dicamus, nihil videtur obstare : non quidem quæ unioni prævia intelligatur et ad eam disponens (quod Nestoriani furfuris est), sed illi comes, ad eamque sequens, velut illius ornatus : in qua ipsa nobis idem Christus et auctor exsistat et perfectissimum exemplar ; cum ejus θεουργία, ut Budæo exponitur,
anchorLine: βῇ τρόπον εὗρε τῆς ἀληθοῦς θεουργίας (v). Ὁ δ'
en: 'Of true theurgy.' He seems here to mean true theurgy, or divine operation, which is thus completed by action and contemplation and as it were has the force of both eminently: that is, wisdom, which is nearest to deification. As to how, with Dionysius, theurgy is also said of Christ: nothing seems to prevent it, not indeed as understood to precede the union and dispose toward it (which is of Nestorian chaff), but as its companion and following upon it, like its adornment, in which same [theurgy] Christ is for us both author and most perfect exemplar; with his theurgy, as Budé explains,

text: pro divina miraculorum potestate et operatione paucis fuerit communicata, nec ipsa defuerit Veteri Testamento : secus vero θεουργία, qua sic ad deificationem provehimur, ejusque per Christum renatis omnibus facultas tribuitur. Ipsa angelorum operatio, qua inferiores illuminant ac perficiunt, Dionysio θεουργία, ac si dicas, divinis dotibus imbuens. Ipse Maximus sequenti capite clare explicat, sic ex ambobus provenientem sapientiam ; in qua statuit salutis nostræ mysterium (θεουργική scilicet) quo sic deitate imbuimur.
anchorLine: continuation of note (v) from p-0684 (call at τῆς ἀληθοῦς θεουργίας (v) on that page)
en: (Continuing from the previous page: '...as Budé explains,') '...[a theurgy] for the divine power and operation of miracles granted to few, and one that was not lacking to the Old Testament; but the theurgy by which we are raised to deification, the capacity for which is given to all reborn through Christ. The operation of the angels itself, by which the lower illuminate and perfect, is for Dionysius theurgy, as if you were to say 'endowing with divine gifts'. Maximus himself explains clearly in the next chapter that wisdom thus proceeds from both; in which he places the mystery of our salvation (the theurgic, that is), by which we are thus imbued with deity.'

text: Δ[...]ξαν δὲ βί[...]. Claritatem reddidi ; Picus, opinionem. At, quid hic vitæ opinio, ut hoc ratio seu scientia illi dicatur ? Ejus vero claritatem esse seu gloriam, res perspicua sit, cum vita, ejus solum exhibitio sit ac manifestatio. Quod enim ratio ad vitam Maximo comparatur ut anima ad corpus, et ut vitam ei præstans, sine qua inane simulacrum sit, εἴδωλον, ejus plane nobilitas et gloria et claritas est, δόξα, non frigidum illud, opinio.
anchorLine: μὲν λόγου, τὸν βίον (x), δόξαν δὲ βίου, τὸν λόγον
en: '[Glory/δόξα of life].' I have rendered it 'clarity'; Picus [rendered it] 'opinion'. But what would 'opinion of life' be here, that reason or knowledge should be called that for it? That its clarity is rather its glory is plain, since life is only its exhibition and manifestation. For since in Maximus reason is compared to life as soul to body, and as the thing that gives it life, without which it would be an empty image (εἴδωλον), its plain nobility, glory and brightness is δόξα, not that cold thing, 'opinion'.

text: Μετενέγκας πρὸς τὸν νοῦν τοῖς λόγοις τὴν αἴσθησιν. Altissime hic Maximo explicata, mentis in sensum sensusque in mentem vicaria munia. Nempe sensus rationibus in mentem transfertur, ut ipse conjunctione cum illa velut intelligat : mens vero scite miroque artificio rerum figuris ac formis, seu speciebus, sensui innectitur, iisque quasi vinculis ad eum trahitur ; μετεγκλοιώσας quod nempe non intelligat pro hoc statu, nisi conversione ad phantasmata, ut philosophus loquitur ; quorum necessitudine a nativa puræ mentis ac solutæ ingenuitate ad sensus compositionem velut desciscat, illiusque qualitatem induat. Ducta metaphora a canibus, quorum sunt κλ[...]ὶ illi et collaria, quibus ad nutum trahentis aguntur, dicuntur et reorum catenæ et vincula.
anchorLine: πρὸς τὸν νοῦν τοῖς λόγοις τὴν αἴσθησιν (y), ἐν δὲ τῷ
en: 'Having carried sense over to mind by the reasons.' Explained very deeply here by Maximus: the reciprocal offices of mind into sense and of sense into mind. Sense, that is, is carried over into mind through the reasons, so that by conjunction with it it as it were itself understands; mind, in turn, is by a skilful and wonderful device bound to sense by the figures and forms (species) of things, and drawn to it as by chains; [the word] μετεγκλοιώσας ('collared/chained across'), namely because it does not understand in this present state except by turning to phantasms, as the philosopher says; by their bond it as it were falls away from the native, unconstrained freedom of the pure mind to composition with sense and takes on its quality. The metaphor is drawn from dogs, which have their κλ[...] (collars) and collars by which they are led at the will of the one who pulls; the word is also used of the chains and fetters of prisoners.

text: Αἰσχύνη στόματος. Expositio est nominis Μεμφιβο[...]θὲ alterius filiorum Saulis ex Rhespha pellice; ut et ἀνάθημα (seu potius ἀνάθεμα, ut quæst. illa 65 scribitur) alterius, nempe Ἐρον[...] : quos ambos Maximus illaudatæ sobolis typo accipit, quippe ex illegitimo susceptos connubio : nec raro ἀναγωγίαν sensumque spiritalem in ejusmodi nominum Hebraicorum etymologia fundat; quam et methodum exponendi Scripturas in his ipsis Capitibus commendat. Nihil ad rem, quod Picus, illud Αἰσχύνη στόματος, dictu pudendu, dictu infamis reddit, ac si esset sequentis vocis, μελέτη vel κίνησις epithetum : τὸ ἀνάθημα non habuit, mutilo ipsi textu : ac nec forte nobis omnino integer repræsentatur. Plura in illa Quæst. in textu ipso et in Scholiis.
anchorLine: κβʹ. Αἰσχύνη στόματός (z) ἐστιν, ἡ κατὰ νοῦν
en: 'Shame of the mouth.' [This is] an explanation of the name Mephibosheth, the other of Saul's sons by the concubine Rizpah; and likewise of ἀνάθημα (or rather ἀνάθεμα, as it is written in that question 65) of the other, namely [Eron...]: both of whom Maximus takes as a type of disreputable offspring, since they were born of an illegitimate union; and he often grounds the anagogy and spiritual sense on the etymology of such Hebrew names, a method of interpreting Scripture which he also commends in these very chapters. It is beside the point that Picus renders 'Αἰσχύνη στόματος' as 'shameful to say, infamous to say', as if it were an epithet of the following word, μελέτη or κίνησις; he lacked τὸ ἀνάθημα, the text being mutilated: and perhaps even for us it is not handed down wholly intact. More on this in that Question, in the text itself, and in the Scholia.
